entries.lesson_title: Periodic Signals as Sums of Sinusoids
entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret a periodic continuous-time signal as a weighted sum of sinusoidal harmonic components organized around a fundamental frequency.

sections.lesson_title: Periodic Signals as Sums of Sinusoids
sections.section_title: Introduction to Periodic Signals as Sums of Sinusoids

blocks.text: A periodic continuous-time signal can be read as a weighted sum of sinusoidal harmonic components organized around a fundamental frequency. The constant part is the DC term, and the oscillating parts sit at frequencies $k\omega_0$ with weights that tell how much of each harmonic is present.

This is the smallest usable case: one constant offset plus the first harmonic at $\omega_0$. Read the constant term as the DC component and read the sinusoidal terms as the first weighted harmonic contribution.

Higher harmonics follow the same pattern at $2\omega_0$, $3\omega_0$, and beyond. The next sections will use this lens to identify one component, read its weight, and then interpret a full harmonic sum as one periodic waveform.

sections.lesson_title: Periodic Signals as Sums of Sinusoids
sections.section_title: Identifying One Sinusoidal Component in a Periodic Signal

example_content.example_prompt: Given $x(t)=3+2\cos(\omega_0 t)-\sin(2\omega_0 t)$, identify one sinusoidal component and state which harmonic it is.

explanation_blocks.text: A single sinusoidal component is identified by its frequency $k\omega_0$, not by its coefficient alone. In a harmonic-sum description, the DC term sits separately and each sinusoid is tagged by its harmonic frequency.
Now apply that rule to $x(t)=3+2\cos(\omega_0 t)-\sin(2\omega_0 t)$. The DC term is $3$, so the first harmonic sinusoidal component is $2\cos(\omega_0 t)$.

That component has harmonic index $k=1$, so its frequency is $\omega_0$. The coefficient $2$ is the weight on that harmonic, while the term $-\sin(2\omega_0 t)$ is the second harmonic at $2\omega_0$. Read the frequency first, then name the term it identifies.

sections.lesson_title: Periodic Signals as Sums of Sinusoids
sections.section_title: Interpreting Weights on Sinusoidal Components

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=1+\tfrac{3}{2}\cos(\omega_0 t)-\tfrac{1}{2}\sin(2\omega_0 t)+4\cos(3\omega_0 t)$, explain what the weight on each sinusoidal component says about its contribution.

explanation_blocks.text: In a harmonic-sum description, each coefficient is the weight on its sinusoidal component. Compare the weights by magnitude first; the sign can change orientation or phase, but it does not change the fact that the term is present.

Now apply that rule to $x(t)=1+\tfrac{3}{2}\cos(\omega_0 t)-\tfrac{1}{2}\sin(2\omega_0 t)+4\cos(3\omega_0 t)$. The weights have magnitudes $\tfrac{3}{2}$, $\tfrac{1}{2}$, and $4$, so the $3\omega_0$ term is the strongest contribution.

The coefficient $4$ is the largest magnitude, so $4\cos(3\omega_0 t)$ contributes most strongly. The minus sign on $-\tfrac{1}{2}\sin(2\omega_0 t)$ changes the term's orientation, but it is still a smaller contribution than the $3\omega_0$ harmonic. Read coefficient magnitude as weight and keep the harmonic frequency fixed while comparing terms.

sections.lesson_title: Periodic Signals as Sums of Sinusoids
sections.section_title: Interpreting a Sum of Harmonic Sinusoids

example_content.example_prompt: Given $x(t)=2+\cos(\omega_0 t)-\tfrac{1}{2}\sin(\omega_0 t)+\tfrac{3}{4}\cos(2\omega_0 t)$, interpret the signal as a sum of harmonic sinusoids and identify which frequencies appear.

explanation_blocks.text: Start by reading the whole expression as one periodic signal. The constant term $2$ is the DC part, and the remaining terms sit at harmonic frequencies of the same fundamental spacing.

Now apply that grouping to $x(t)=2+\cos(\omega_0 t)-\tfrac{1}{2}\sin(\omega_0 t)+\tfrac{3}{4}\cos(2\omega_0 t)$. The terms at $\omega_0$ are $\cos(\omega_0 t)$ and $-\tfrac{1}{2}\sin(\omega_0 t)$, and the next harmonic is $\tfrac{3}{4}\cos(2\omega_0 t)$.
So the signal contains frequency components at $0$, $\omega_0$, and $2\omega_0$. Read the full sum as one periodic waveform built from the DC term and integer multiples of the fundamental frequency.

sections.lesson_title: Periodic Signals as Sums of Sinusoids
sections.section_title: Relating a Sinusoidal Sum to the Periodic Waveform

example_content.example_prompt: Given a harmonic sum such as $x(t)=1+2\cos(\omega_0 t)-\tfrac{1}{2}\sin(2\omega_0 t)$, describe the waveform features implied by the DC term and the harmonic weights.

explanation_blocks.text: Start by reading the sum as the waveform description itself. The constant term $1$ sets the vertical offset, and the largest harmonic term usually controls the main oscillation you notice first.

Now apply that rule to $x(t)=1+2\cos(\omega_0 t)-\tfrac{1}{2}\sin(2\omega_0 t)$. The waveform is centered at $1$, the $2\cos(\omega_0 t)$ term gives the strongest up-and-down motion, and the $2\omega_0$ term adds a smaller distortion to the shape.

So the signal is one periodic waveform, not separate pieces. It repeats with the same fundamental spacing, but the second harmonic makes the shape less purely sinusoidal than $2\cos(\omega_0 t)$ alone.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the DC component of a periodic signal as its average value over one period and interpret it as the zero-frequency term in a Fourier series.

sections.section_title: Introduction to DC Component

blocks.text: The DC component of a periodic signal is the constant part of the waveform: the average value you get over one full period, written as `$x_{\mathrm{DC}}$`.
Because the signal is periodic, you can start that average at any time $t_0$ as long as the interval length is $T_0$. The average does not change when you slide the window by whole periods.
For the base case $x(t)=C$, the average returns the same constant, so the definition matches the idea of a flat signal: its DC component is just the level it sits at.

In Fourier series language, that average is the zero-frequency term. Later examples will compute the same quantity from signed areas and vertical offsets, but the rule is already here: average one period, and you have the DC component.

sections.section_title: Computing the Average Value Over One Period

example_content.example_prompt: Let $x(t)=4$ for $0 \le t < T_0/4$ and $x(t)=0$ for $T_0/4 \le t < T_0$, repeated every $T_0$. Find the DC component.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a periodic piecewise-constant signal, so the DC component is still the average value over one period. Use the same rule from the previous step: average the signal over any interval of length $T_0$.

Over one period, the signal is $4$ on the first quarter and $0$ on the remaining three quarters. That means we compute signed area by weighting each level by how long it lasts, not by averaging the heights alone.
So the DC component is $1$. In Fourier series language, that is the zero-frequency term: the constant level left after the waveform is averaged over one period.

sections.section_title: Recognizing a Zero DC Component from Balanced Areas

example_content.example_prompt: Let $x(t)=2$ for $0 \le t < T_0/3$ and $x(t)=-1$ for $T_0/3 \le t < T_0$, repeated every $T_0$. Find the DC component.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a periodic piecewise-constant signal with one positive level and one negative level, so the DC component comes from signed area over one period. Use the same average formula as before and check whether the positive and negative contributions cancel.
The positive contribution is $\frac{2T_0}{3}$ and the negative contribution is $-\frac{2T_0}{3}$. They have equal magnitude, so the signed areas cancel before the division by $T_0$.
So the DC component is $0$. The waveform is not zero everywhere, but its one-period average is zero, so the zero-frequency term in the Fourier series vanishes.

sections.section_title: Computing a Nonzero DC Component from Vertical Offset

example_content.example_prompt: Let $q(t)=2$ for $0 \le t < T_0/3$ and $q(t)=-1$ for $T_0/3 \le t < T_0$, and define $x(t)=3+q(t)$. Find the DC component of $x(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the decomposition $x(t)=3+q(t)$. Treat $3$ as the constant vertical offset and $q(t)$ as the balanced periodic variation. The DC component is the one-period average, so average the two parts separately.
From the previous step, the variation $q(t)$ has zero average because its positive and negative areas cancel over one period. That means only the constant baseline survives the averaging.
So the DC component is $3$. The vertical offset is exactly the zero-frequency term, while the balanced waveform contributes no additional DC component.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the DC Component as the Zero-Frequency Term

example_content.example_prompt: Given the trigonometric Fourier series $x(t)=\frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(n\omega_0 t)+b_n\sin(n\omega_0 t)\big)$, identify the DC component and explain why it is the zero-frequency term.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the standard trigonometric Fourier-series form. The DC component is the constant term, so look for the piece with no oscillation: $\frac{a_0}{2}$.
Every term in the sum has $n\ge 1$, so each one is a harmonic at nonzero frequency. Those sine and cosine terms average to zero over one period, so they do not contribute to the DC component.
So the DC component is the zero-frequency term $\frac{a_0}{2}$. A frequency-$0$ term does not oscillate, so it matches the constant average-value part of the signal.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the Fourier-series fundamental frequency \(\omega_0 = 2\pi/T_0\) from a periodic signal's period and use it as the spacing between harmonic components.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Fundamental Frequency in Fourier Series

blocks.text: A Fourier series is read on a frequency grid. The key quantity on that grid is the fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0$, because every harmonic component sits at an integer multiple of that spacing.

If a periodic signal repeats every $T_0$ seconds, then one full cycle corresponds to the same $2\pi$ radians of phase each time. That is why the period tells you the spacing of the Fourier-series frequency grid.

Use the simplest base case first: if $T_0 = 1$ s, then $\omega_0 = 2\pi$ rad/s. The harmonic locations then appear at $0,\omega_0,2\omega_0,3\omega_0,\dots$, so the spacing between adjacent components is always the same fundamental step.
So the reusable procedure is simple: find $T_0$ first, convert it to $\omega_0$, and then use $\omega_0$ to read the spacing between the harmonic components in the Fourier-series description.

sections.section_title: Computing omega_0 from a Given Fundamental Period

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal has $T_0 = 2$ s. Compute its fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the fundamental period $T_0$. Once $T_0$ is known, the fundamental angular frequency comes from direct substitution into $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T_0$.
Now simplify the result. With $T_0 = 2$ s, the spacing is $\pi$ rad/s, so the Fourier-series frequency grid advances in steps of $\pi$.

sections.section_title: Computing omega_0 After Identifying the Fundamental Period

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic waveform repeats on intervals of length $3$ s. Identify $T_0$ and compute $\omega_0$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the repeat description. A waveform that repeats every $3$ s has fundamental period $T_0 = 3$ s.
Now apply the rule $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T_0$ and substitute the identified period.
So the fundamental angular frequency is $\omega_0 = \frac{2\pi}{3}$ rad/s. That is the spacing used by the Fourier-series harmonic grid.

sections.section_title: Using omega_0 as the Spacing Between Fourier Series Frequencies

example_content.example_prompt: If $\omega_0 = \pi/3$ rad/s, list the first four nonnegative Fourier-series frequencies and show how the spacing works.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the given spacing $\omega_0$. For Fourier series, the frequencies form an equally spaced grid at integer multiples of $\omega_0$.
Substitute $\omega_0 = \pi/3$ rad/s. For the first four nonnegative grid points, use $k = 0, 1, 2, 3$.
So each adjacent harmonic is separated by $\pi/3$ rad/s, which is the same spacing as $\omega_0$.

sections.section_title: Comparing Frequency Spacing for Different Fundamental Periods

example_content.example_prompt: Signal A has $T_0 = 2$ s and signal B has $T_0 = 4$ s. Compute each $\omega_0$ and state which harmonic grid is more widely spaced.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the period. Fundamental frequency changes inversely with $T_0$, so the shorter period gives the wider spacing.
For Signal A, substitute $T_0 = 2$ s into the rule.
For Signal B, substitute $T_0 = 4$ s into the same rule.
Signal A has the larger spacing, and it is twice Signal B's spacing. That is the inverse period-spacing relationship.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute harmonic frequencies as integer multiples of the fundamental frequency and interpret each multiple as a sinusoidal component in the Fourier-series frequency-domain view.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Harmonic Frequencies

blocks.text: Once the fundamental frequency $\omega_0$ is known, harmonic frequencies are the positive integer multiples of that same spacing. In the Fourier-series frequency-domain view, those multiples are the discrete frequencies you read off as separate sinusoidal components.
Here $k$ is the harmonic index, and it is a positive integer. Start with $k=1$ so the first harmonic is just $\omega_0$, then use the same rule for $k=2$, $k=3$, and beyond.

This gives a simple ladder of equally spaced harmonic frequencies: each new harmonic is one more copy of the fundamental spacing. The pattern is always the same rule, multiply $\omega_0$ by the integer index.

So when you look at a Fourier-series spectrum, treat each nonzero harmonic line as one sinusoidal component at $\omega_k = k\omega_0$. The $0$-frequency DC term is separate from the harmonic frequencies.

sections.section_title: Computing Harmonic Frequencies from a Fundamental Frequency

example_content.example_prompt: Given $\omega_0 = 3\pi$ rad/s and $k = 4$, compute the fourth harmonic frequency.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the integer harmonic index $k$. Use the rule from the introduction, $\omega_k = k\omega_0$, and substitute the given values for $k$ and $\omega_0$.
So the fourth harmonic frequency is $12\pi$ rad/s. The only operation is multiplying the fundamental frequency by the harmonic index.

sections.section_title: Listing the First Several Harmonic Frequencies

example_content.example_prompt: List the first five harmonic frequencies when $\omega_0 = 2\pi$ rad/s.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the request to list several harmonics. Use the same rule from the previous example, $\omega_k = k\omega_0$, and start with $k=1$ so the list begins at the first harmonic.
So the first five harmonic frequencies are $2\pi$, $4\pi$, $6\pi$, $8\pi$, and $10\pi$ rad/s in ascending order. Each entry is an integer multiple of the same fundamental frequency.

sections.section_title: Matching Frequencies to Harmonic Indices

example_content.example_prompt: If $\omega_0 = 5\pi$ rad/s, which harmonic index corresponds to $20\pi$ rad/s?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the target frequency $20\pi$ rad/s. To match a frequency to a harmonic index, compare it to the spacing frequency $\omega_0$ and form the ratio $\omega / \omega_0$.
The ratio is the integer $4$, so the frequency is exactly $4\omega_0$. The matching harmonic index is $k=4$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Harmonics as Frequency-Domain Components

example_content.example_prompt: A Fourier-series spectrum has lines at $\omega_0$, $3\omega_0$, and $5\omega_0$. Which harmonic components are present, and what do they mean?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a set of spectral lines at integer multiples of $\omega_0$. In the Fourier-series frequency-domain view, each line is one sinusoidal component at a harmonic frequency.
So the spectrum contains the 1st, 3rd, and 5th harmonic components. Each allowed line marks one sinusoidal component in the harmonic decomposition.

entries.lesson_core_move: Identify sine and cosine waves at integer multiples of the fundamental frequency as basis functions whose weighted combination represents a periodic signal.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Sine and Cosine Basis Functions

blocks.text: This step is about the basis-function view of the trigonometric Fourier series, not about computing coefficients. The objects to recognize are the sine and cosine waves at integer multiples of the fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0$; the coefficients that appear later are weights, not basis functions.

Start with the first harmonic pair, $\cos(\omega_0 t)$ and $\sin(\omega_0 t)$. Once you see the $k=1$ case, the same pattern extends to every harmonic by substituting $k=2,3,\dots$ into the same sine and cosine arguments.

The key action is to separate the basis waves from the coefficients. The basis functions tell you which trigonometric waves are available; the coefficients only tell you how much of each wave is present.

So when you read a trigonometric Fourier series, identify each harmonic pair by its integer multiple of $\omega_0$, then treat the coefficients as the weights that build the periodic signal from those basis functions.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Fundamental Sine and Cosine Basis Pair

example_content.example_prompt: For a periodic signal with fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0$, identify the sine and cosine basis functions that make up the first harmonic pair.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is the first harmonic pair, so read the harmonic index as $k=1$. In the trigonometric Fourier-series basis view, each harmonic uses the same two families: the cosine and sine terms at $k\omega_0$.
Now substitute $k=1$ into both families. That gives the basis functions for the fundamental harmonic.

So the fundamental sine and cosine basis pair is $\cos(\omega_0 t)$ and $\sin(\omega_0 t)$. These are the basis waves themselves; the coefficients that appear later are only the weights on these two functions.

sections.section_title: Identifying Sine and Cosine Basis Functions at Higher Harmonics

example_content.example_prompt: Identify the sine and cosine basis functions for the $k=3$ harmonic of a signal with fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the harmonic index $k=3$. Keep the same basis-function pattern from the earlier example and substitute $k=3$ into the cosine and sine families.
Now replace $k$ with $3$ in both arguments. The harmonic number changes the frequency multiplier, but it does not change the basis-function pattern.
So the third-harmonic basis pair is $\cos(3\omega_0 t)$ and $\sin(3\omega_0 t)$. These are the basis waves before any coefficients are applied.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Weights on Harmonic Sine and Cosine Basis Functions

example_content.example_prompt: Given the terms $4\cos(2\omega_0 t)-7\sin(2\omega_0 t)$, identify the weights on the $k=2$ sine and cosine basis functions.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the harmonic index $k=2$. Read each weight from the number in front of the matching basis function and keep the sign attached to that coefficient.
The cosine term carries the weight $a_2=4$. The sine term carries the weight $b_2=-7$, so the sign stays with the sine coefficient.
So the coefficient pair is $(a_2,b_2)=(4,-7)$. The basis pair remains the $k=2$ harmonic; only the weights are being read off.

sections.section_title: Interpreting a Periodic Signal as a Weighted Sum of Harmonic Basis Functions

example_content.example_prompt: Interpret the signal $x(t)=\frac{a_0}{2}+a_1\cos(\omega_0 t)+b_1\sin(\omega_0 t)+a_2\cos(2\omega_0 t)+b_2\sin(2\omega_0 t)$ as a weighted sum of harmonic basis functions.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the expanded trigonometric Fourier series. Start by separating the DC term from the harmonic terms, then group each cosine and sine pair by its shared harmonic index.

The $k=1$ cosine and sine terms form one weighted basis pair, and the $k=2$ cosine and sine terms form the next weighted basis pair. The coefficients stay attached to the correct function and harmonic index.

So the periodic signal is the DC term plus a sum of weighted harmonic basis pairs. This is the reusable basis-function view: the sine and cosine terms are the basis functions, and the coefficients are their weights.

entries.lesson_core_move: Translate a periodic signal between its time-domain waveform and frequency-domain harmonic description by identifying how DC, fundamental frequency, harmonic frequencies, and sine/cosine basis components encode the same signal.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time-Domain vs. Frequency-Domain Views

blocks.text: A periodic signal can be read in two equivalent ways: as a time-domain waveform and as a frequency-domain harmonic description. The signal does not change; only the representation changes.
In the time-domain view, you look at $x(t)$ as a waveform across one period. In the frequency-domain view, you list the DC term and the harmonic components at integer multiples of $\omega_0$.

Start with the simplest base case: one DC term and one fundamental harmonic. That base case lets you match the constant offset to the zero-frequency term and the oscillating part to the first harmonic without extra algebra.

The shared landmarks are $a_0$, $\omega_0$, and $k\omega_0$: $a_0$ is the DC component, $\omega_0$ sets the spacing between harmonics, and $k\omega_0$ identifies the $k$th harmonic. The sine and cosine terms are the basis pieces that encode the same periodic signal in frequency form.

Read the later sections as translations between these views. Each time you move from waveform to harmonic list, you are describing the same signal in a different language, not introducing a different signal.

sections.section_title: Reading DC and Fundamental Frequency Across Views

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal has $x(t)=3+2\cos(\omega_0 t)$. Identify its DC term and fundamental angular frequency, then state how those show up in the frequency-domain description.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the constant term in $x(t)=3+2\cos(\omega_0 t)$. A constant offset does not oscillate, so it is the DC term, and here $a_0=3$.
The oscillating part is the cosine at angular frequency $\omega_0$. That makes $\omega_0$ the fundamental angular frequency, the first harmonic spacing in the frequency-domain view.

Read the same signal as a frequency-domain description with a zero-frequency term and a harmonic at $\omega_0$. The constant part becomes the DC component, and the cosine part becomes the first harmonic.
So the frequency-domain side says: DC term $a_0=3$ and fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0$. The amplitude 2 is the weight on that fundamental cosine component.
This is the key translation: the waveform's baseline and first oscillation are not separate ideas, just the same signal read in two representations.

sections.section_title: Reading Harmonic Frequencies Across Views

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal is given by $x(t)=1+4\cos(\omega_0 t)-2\sin(3\omega_0 t)$. Which harmonic frequencies appear in its frequency-domain description, and which term corresponds to each frequency?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the frequency inside each sinusoid, not the size of its coefficient. The constant term $1$ is the DC component, so $a_0=1$.
The term $4\cos(\omega_0 t)$ is the first harmonic, because its angular frequency is $\omega_0$. The term $-2\sin(3\omega_0 t)$ is the third harmonic, because its angular frequency is $3\omega_0$.

So the frequency-domain description contains a zero-frequency term, a line at $\omega_0$, and a line at $3\omega_0$. The coefficient values 4 and -2 change the weights on those lines, not the harmonic locations.
There is no $2\omega_0$ line, because no term in the waveform uses that harmonic. Reading the frequency-domain view is just naming the frequencies actually present in the time-domain sum.

sections.section_title: Matching Sine and Cosine Basis Components Across Views

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal is described by the frequency-domain coefficients $a_1=2$, $b_1=-1$, and $a_2=3$ with $a_0=0$. Write the equivalent time-domain Fourier-series form.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the coefficient label attached to each harmonic, not the waveform shape. Since $a_0=0$, there is no DC term. The coefficients $a_k$ belong to cosine terms and the coefficients $b_k$ belong to sine terms at the same harmonic index.
So $a_1=2$ becomes $2\cos(\omega_0 t)$, $b_1=-1$ becomes $-\sin(\omega_0 t)$, and $a_2=3$ becomes $3\cos(2\omega_0 t)$. The sign stays with the coefficient, and the harmonic index stays on the angle.

explanation_blocks.latex: a_0=0,\quad a_1=2,\quad b_1=-1,\quad a_2=3 \;\Longrightarrow\; x(t)=2\cos(\omega_0 t)-\sin(\omega_0 t)+3\cos(2\omega_0 t)

explanation_blocks.text: The assembled time-domain form uses the same harmonic content in basis-function form: first harmonic cosine, first harmonic sine, and second harmonic cosine. Nothing changes except the representation.

This is the matching rule students should reuse: read the coefficient label, choose cosine or sine, place it at the correct $k\omega_0$, and preserve the sign. That reconstructs the time-domain Fourier-series expression directly from the frequency-domain coefficients.

sections.section_title: Translating a Full Periodic Signal Description Across Views

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal is given by $x(t)=2+3\cos(\omega_0 t)-\sin(\omega_0 t)+4\cos(2\omega_0 t)$. State the matching frequency-domain harmonic description and then read the same signal back from that description.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is to read each coefficient together with its harmonic and basis type. In $x(t)=2+3\cos(\omega_0 t)-\sin(\omega_0 t)+4\cos(2\omega_0 t)$, the constant term is the DC component, the $\cos(\omega_0 t)$ and $\sin(\omega_0 t)$ terms belong to the first harmonic, and the $\cos(2\omega_0 t)$ term belongs to the second harmonic.

explanation_blocks.latex: x(t)=2+3\cos(\omega_0 t)-\sin(\omega_0 t)+4\cos(2\omega_0 t)\;\Longrightarrow\; a_0=2,\quad a_1=3,\quad b_1=-1,\quad a_2=4

explanation_blocks.text: So the frequency-domain reading keeps the same information but names it by coefficient labels: DC is $a_0=2$, first-harmonic cosine is $a_1=3$, first-harmonic sine is $b_1=-1$, and second-harmonic cosine is $a_2=4$.

explanation_blocks.latex: a_0=2,\quad a_1=3,\quad b_1=-1,\quad a_2=4\;\Longrightarrow\; x(t)=2+3\cos(\omega_0 t)-\sin(\omega_0 t)+4\cos(2\omega_0 t)

explanation_blocks.text: The result is a one-to-one translation: preserve the DC term, preserve the harmonic index, choose sine or cosine correctly, and keep the sign on the coefficient. That is the full cross-view match the student should imitate.
